item.title: Will AI Replace Juniors? How Task Complexity Reduces Automation Risk
item.description: arXiv:2611.34099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Rost, Fabian Stephany

item.title: Optimization of a Hybrid Solar-Biogas-Battery Energy Storage Microgrid: A Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.33593v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-income regions like eastern Uganda often lack reliable grid power. This paper presents the techno-economic optimization of the Soroti Integrated Renewable Energy Microgrid (SIREM), a hybrid renewable system for grid-access expansion where Soroti District household grid access stands at 16.7\%. The microgrid integrates concentrating solar power (CSP) with thermal storage, biogas combined cycle generation, and lithium iron phosphate battery storage. Using Xendee optimization software with six years of NASA POWER data, the optimal configuration comprises a 37 MW CSP field, 70 MWh molten-salt storage, a 5 MW CSP turbine, a 6 MW biogas CCGT, and a 10 MWh battery system. The design delivers 61.3 GWh annually with a 42.91% IRR, 2-year payback, and levelized cost of electricity of 0.1991 USD/kWh generation (0.3752 USD/kWh load-served), achieving 32.2% total savings versus grid-only supply while exporting 28.8 GWh annually, demonstrating the viability of hybrid renewable microgrids for grid expansion in sub-Saharan Africa.
item.dc:creator: John Elomunait, Jesse Thornburg

item.title: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding
item.description: arXiv:2611.34068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.

item.title: AI and the Division of Labor in Public Sector Jobs and Teams
item.description: arXiv:2512.05659v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How artificial intelligence (AI) affects an organization depends not only on which jobs are exposed, but on how more (versus less) exposed tasks are combined within roles. Using 283,484 UK Civil Service vacancies, we extract 2.7 million tasks and estimate their automation potential with an ensemble of eight foundation models. We find that differences among tasks within roles account for 65.3 percent of total exposure variance, while profession and grade together explain only 4.0 percent, suggesting that seemingly similar roles often differ substantially in their exposure and potential for redesign. Combining roles' mean exposure with their within-role dispersion distinguishes where workforce adjustment, job redesign, targeted task automation, or limited intervention may be most relevant. Taking account of which tasks can change as AI expands into a role, we simulate redesign at the role and team level. Role redesign cuts administration from 30.0 to 24.6 percent of working time and raises assurance tasks from 8.7 to 14.5 percent. When conducted at the team level, redesign merges overlapping roles, cutting the number of distinct roles by 17.7 percent while headcount falls by only 6.4 percent; the posts removed come from junior and middle grades, so restructured teams become weighted toward senior staff. We contribute to the automation, augmentation and productivity debates and advance our understanding of job redesign in the age of AI.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Ledingham, Michael Hollins, Matthew Lyon, David Gillespie, Umar Yunis-Guerra, Jamie Siviter, David Duncan, Oliver P. Hauser

item.title: Macroeconomic Risks from Maritime Trade Disruptions
item.description: arXiv:2607.09951v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a model of maritime chokepoint closures in which interrupting a shipping passage produces losses that are not measured, or even bounded, by the value of the trade that transits it. The losses stem from disruptions to the flow of intermediate inputs that are complementary in downstream production. They travel through the world trade network, which itself rewires around the closed passage. Re-matching displaced trade on the buyer and seller sides of the market, which the model carries out as rationing at fixed prices, limits the damage but does not eliminate it. Across countries, the incidence of these losses is heavy-tailed, and it reaches economies that sell nothing through the passage, some of which buy little through it either. The two ends of a severed corridor lose unequally. At the typical corridor the economies that mainly sell through it lose more than twice as much as those that mainly buy through it, and at the largest energy gate between four and five times as much, as economic geography funnels commodity-concentrated sellers through a single passage while their buyers re-source. Economic geography decides how the loss from closing several chokepoints together compares with the sum of the losses from closing each alone. A shipment stopped at the first of two gates in series cannot be stopped again at the second, so such gates duplicate one another, whereas gates in parallel take different cargo for the most part, so their losses add. Which is why the Middle East scenario costs about a tenth less than the sum of its single closures, while the East Asian and Russia-Europe scenarios cost that sum to within three percent.
item.dc:creator: Vipin P. Veetil, Fathimath S. Vemmarath
